source.title_on_document: Long-term impact of ChatGPT-4 on music students' creative and analytical skills: A follow-up study

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Data are available on request from the corresponding author (p. 17, Data availability).

paper_design_summary: Seventy-four second-year Bachelor of Music students in South Korea were assigned, at the class level, to a group that used ChatGPT-4 in weekly composition, improvisation, harmonic analysis, transcription, and arranging tasks (n = 36) or to traditional teacher-led instruction (n = 38) for 24 weeks. Two blinded external assessors scored the creative products and analytical tasks submitted every two weeks (12 measurement points) on 7-point rubrics of creativity and analytical thinking. The paper compares growth trajectories (latent growth models) and covariate-adjusted end scores (MANCOVA), and also codes the experimental group's ChatGPT interaction logs.

studies.label: 24-week classroom intervention: ChatGPT-4 versus traditional instruction in a Bachelor of Music programme

assignment.what_was_assigned: Instruction with ChatGPT-4 integrated into weekly music tasks versus traditional teacher-led instruction without AI; assignment was at the class level. The paper calls the design quasi-experimental and does not state how many classes there were.
assignment.quote: In the present study, participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups. ... While the random assignment was conducted at the class level (an unavoidable constraint of the institutional timetable)
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1 (Design and participants); p. 5: 'The study adopted a quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test design.'

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT-4)
arms.description: Integrated ChatGPT-4 into weekly composition, improvisation, harmonic analysis, transcription, and arranging tasks: generating melodic or harmonic suggestions, drafting programme notes, receiving simulated feedback (Table 1, p. 6; Section 3.2, p. 5).

arms.name: Control (traditional instruction)
arms.description: Equivalent tasks with textbooks, class notes, lectures, handouts, and teacher consultation; feedback from the instructor without AI. Same instructor as the experimental group (pp. 5-6).

participants.exclusions: None reported. Of 86 students in the music programme, 12 took part in the pilot study and not in the main study (p. 5). Table 6 (p. 12) lists N = 36 and 38, and the univariate tests have df2 = 69 (Table 5), consistent with all 74 analyzed.
participants.who: Second-year undergraduates in a Bachelor of Music programme; drawn from the cohort of the authors' earlier short-term ChatGPT-4 study (Zhou & Kim, 2024).
participants.quote: Participants were seventy-four second-year undergraduates enrolled in the Bachelor of Music programme at a university in South Korea.
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1; arm sizes p. 5 and Table 6 (p. 12); abstract (p. 1)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (the paper also refers to GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini as the newer generation, p. 4-5)
ai_tool.how_used: Guided prompts within weekly tasks: ChatGPT-4 supplied melodic, structural, and improvisation ideas, alternative harmonic progressions and reharmonizations, checks of rhythmic and harmonic accuracy, arrangement suggestions, and feedback on drafts; students were asked to evaluate, adapt, and integrate the output and to submit screenshots or links of their interactions (Table 1, p. 6; Sections 3.2 and 3.6, pp. 5-8).

task.description: Music tasks: melody writing and composition, improvisation, harmonic analysis and reharmonization, stylistic transcription, and arranging; every two weeks each student submitted a creative product (composition or improvisation) and an analytical task. 'creative_writing' is the nearest code; the task is musical composition, which could also be coded 'other'.
task.duration: 24 weeks over two semesters (October 2024 to January 2025 and March to June 2025); 12 measurement points

outcomes.name: Creativity rubric score of submitted music products
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric adapted from Webster (2002) and Burnard's (2012) use of the Consensual Assessment Technique; four dimensions on a seven-point scale (originality of musical ideas, overall musical value, inventiveness in development, expressive impact), scored by two blinded external assessors with expertise in music theory, composition, and creativity research; discrepancies above two points resolved by discussion (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5). Two analyses: latent growth model of the 12 repeated scores (Table 3) and MANCOVA/ANCOVA with prior ChatGPT use and Week 1 creativity and analytical scores as covariates (Tables 4-6). The paper does not state which time point the MANCOVA dependent variable uses. Cross-lagged panel results (Table 7) compare paths, not levels.
outcomes.delay: Repeated over 24 weeks; products scored during the intervention while the experimental group used ChatGPT-4

contrasts.reported: Adjusted means: Experimental 4.71 (Std. Error 0.18, N = 36) vs Control 4.35 (Std. Error 0.17, N = 38). Univariate Group effect on creativity F(1, 69) = 7.216, p = .009, eta^2 = .096. Multivariate Group effect (creativity and analytical combined): Pillai's Trace = .047, F(2, 68) = 3.982, p = .023, eta^2 = .047. Printed spreads are standard errors of adjusted means, not SDs.
contrasts.locator: p. 12, Tables 5 and 6; p. 11, Table 4; p. 9 text (RQ2)

contrasts.reported: Latent growth model, creativity: Experimental intercept 3.281 (Std. Err. 0.043, p < .000), slope 0.315 (0.006, p < .000); Control intercept 3.004 (0.064, p < .000), slope 0.210 (0.010, p < .000). No test of the group difference in slope is printed. Figure 1 plots the estimated trajectories over weeks 1-12.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Table 3; p. 8 text (RQ1); p. 10, Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Analytical thinking rubric score of submitted analytical tasks
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric adapted from Biasutti and Frezza (2009) and Bautista et al. (2018); four dimensions on a seven-point scale (accuracy of harmonic and structural labelling, clarity of theoretical justification, depth of reasoning, transferability of reasoning), scored by the same blinded assessors (p. 7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5). Not a creativity construct; listed because it is the paper's second main outcome.

contrasts.reported: Adjusted means: Experimental 4.67 (Std. Error 0.16, N = 36) vs Control 4.38 (0.16, N = 38); Group F(1, 69) = 5.482, p = .022, eta^2 = .075. Latent growth: Experimental intercept 2.973 (0.038), slope 0.336 (0.005); Control intercept 2.621 (0.056), slope 0.282 (0.009).
contrasts.locator: p. 12, Tables 5 and 6; p. 9, Table 3; p. 11, Fig. 2

sample_overlap.quote: These students were drawn from the cohort involved in our earlier study on the short-term effects of ChatGPT-4 (Zhou & Kim, 2024), thereby providing continuity for a follow-up investigation.

eligibility.reason: The paper states that participants were randomly assigned to two groups, but the randomization was at the class level, the number of classes is not stated (possibly one class per arm), and the paper calls its design quasi-experimental (p. 5). Participants come from an earlier study in which only the AI group received ChatGPT instruction, and the paper does not say whether the earlier groups were kept. The experimental group starts higher at baseline (intercept 3.28 vs 3.00, Table 3). If class-level random assignment is accepted, criteria 2 (74 students analyzed) and 3 (blinded expert ratings of creative products) are met. If it is not, the study is quasi_people (observational context).

one_line_finding: After 24 weeks, music students who used ChatGPT-4 had higher covariate-adjusted creativity scores than students in traditional instruction (4.71 vs 4.35; F(1, 69) = 7.216, p = .009, eta^2 = .096; p. 12, Tables 5-6) and a steeper creativity growth slope (0.315 vs 0.210; p. 9, Table 3).
open_questions: How many classes were randomized, and was each arm a single intact class?
Were the arms the same groups as in Zhou & Kim (2024), where only the AI group received ChatGPT instruction?
Which time point is the MANCOVA dependent variable (final measurement or an average)?
The text cites Tables 1 and 2 for baseline comparability (p. 5), but Table 1 lists instructional themes and Table 2 lists growth-model fit indices; no baseline comparison table is printed.
notes: Only creativity (S1-O1) answers a creativity question. The epistemic network analysis (Figs. 3-4, Table 8) and Markov transition analysis (Figs. 5-6) code the experimental group's ChatGPT interaction logs only (N = 36) and have no control contrast; they are not listed as outcomes. Cross-lagged panel model (Table 7, p. 12): Wald test of group difference in creativity autoregressive path chi2 = 19.16, p < .001, and in analytic-to-creativity path chi2 = 21.47, p < .001; end-point correlation of creativity and analytical r = 0.74 (experimental) vs 0.19 (control). The paper reports p-values as 'p < .000'. The study ran 24 weeks with 12 measurement points every two weeks, but figures and text label the time axis 'Week' 1-12. Fig. 1 shows estimated experimental creativity reaching about 6.7 at the last point, while Table 6 adjusted means are 4.71 and 4.35; the paper does not reconcile the two.
